articles.title: Zoe Kleinman: Nvidia CEO's affair will cause ripples across US and beyond
articles.summary: Jensen Huang is being investigated by his own company over an extramarital affair with a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy.
body: Jensen Huang, 63, has been called the 'Taylor Swift of tech' in the US

The tech world has spent the day digesting the extraordinary news that Jensen Huang - the charismatic, leather-jacket wearing chief executive of the multi-trillion dollar firm Nvidia - is being investigated by his own company over an extramarital affair with a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy.
None of us had that on our bingo cards for 2026.

Huang's alleged romantic affair with Alice Huang (no relation), the former CEO of a Singapore-based data centre company, has cast ripples far beyond his immediate family - undoubtedly on an emotional rollercoaster of their own - taking us to a crossroads at which technology, geopolitics and national security intersect.
In a nutshell, this is about the bitter rivalry between the US and China, as well as whether Jensen Huang has betrayed the US as well as his wife.
"He's suffering": Trump answers BBC question about Nvidia's Jensen Huang
The US is locked in a fierce race with China to develop the best AI models.

"Whoever wins AI, wins," as US President Donald Trump puts it. He thinks that the country with the more dominant AI technology will benefit the most from it and, ultimately, will be the most powerful in the world. He may well be right.
Nvidia happens to make the best chips in the business for AI – so much so that it has been overwhelmed with demand.
It sets its prices accordingly: a single unit of the firm's latest kit for data centres starts at £37,000 ($50,000). A medium or large site might have hundreds of them.
The US administration initially slapped an export ban on Nvidia's more recent devices to prevent China from taking advantage of their superior capabilities. It has since softened the rules a little.

But there are suggestions that Alice Huang's company, Megaspeed, may have been involved in sneaking them into the country while she was in charge. Bloomberg reported that the firm bought billions of dollars worth of Nvidia tech in November 2025. Megaspeed denies that it was used illegitimately.

For his part, Jensen Huang has lobbied heavily for the export rules between the two countries to be relaxed, arguing against the weight of general opinion that the AI race doesn't matter and that it would be no bad thing for China to become dependent on US tech.
"President Trump wants American to win and President Xi wants China to win, and it's possible for both of them to do so," he told the BBC last year.
It think it's safe to assume that neither country sees it that way.
Nvidia shares tumble over investigation into Huang's affair with alleged Chinese spy
Could this be the end of 'Jensanity'

The difficult questions Nvidia now has to try to answer include whether Alice gained special access to the firm's latest technology, either deliberately or not, via Jensen - and, if so, whether she shared it with Beijing or others.

We don't know when their affair began or ended, but there are numerous photos and videos of Jensen and Alice together at events. It is feasible that there were moments when they spent quite a lot of time together and Jensen has talked about always having an eye on his work.
China denies that she was engaged in espionage.

Interest in economic espionage is neither new nor unique to China. But many Western countries say that China does it on a grand scale, using a combination of technology tools and agents embedded in various organisations - including private companies.

China having access to significant enough numbers of Nvidia's chips to make use of them, or stripping them down and learning how to make its own versions, would infuriate the Trump administration, which is trying to keep its AI technology close to its chest.

Some models have even been withheld from the UK-based AI Safety Institute on the grounds that they are potentially too dangerous to be shared. The US does not want anyone having a headstart or misusing its innovations.
Another potential bombshell lies in the form of any national security information to which Jensen Huang may have been privy.

He is a man operating at the very top of the US elite - one of a handful of people who could probably walk into the White House unannounced and have tea with Trump. He has influence, he has access and he has powerful friends. It's quite possible that secrets were shared with him.

Nvidia says there's no evidence so far that he passed anything on and the firm has launched an internal investigation. Huang says he will co-operate and wants to keep his job - though if nothing else, he has broken Nvidia's own code of conduct, which states that company members should not have relationships with clients.

At present, he has the backing of both the Nvidia board and Trump, who described him as "honourable" and speculated that there must have been a reason for what had transpired. In other words, he's not throwing his tech boss buddy under the bus.
Nvidia's share price has fallen but has not tanked spectacularly, suggesting shareholders are not abandoning the company under his stewardship in their droves either.
An AI industry with a weakened Nvidia would undoubtedly be a slower one.
And there isn't really a natural successor waiting in the wings to replace Jensen were he forced out.
Huang has run Nvidia for more than 30 years - to many, he is Nvidia. He has steered it through multiple crises and it was his decision for the firm to focus on AI before it was trendy.

He is known to be a demanding boss who expects staff to work long hours and to high standards. There are stories about him calling all-staff meetings to tell off individuals who had made mistakes. He has said this was to prevent others making the same errors – but you can only imagine how it felt for those on the receiving end.

While he awaits the conclusion of the investigation into his actions, Huang must hope that, despite not tolerating the mistakes of his colleagues in the past, they will be gracious about his own failings.
And he must also live with the irony that he was potentially caught out not by a sophisticated high-tech sting, but by the oldest trick in the book: a honey trap.

articles.title: Inside the French drug gangs recruiting children to kill
articles.summary: The BBC enters Marseille's dangerous underworld, where young people are trapped, brutalised and exploited.
body: Watch: "It destroys people, but we all make our own choices" - Marseille drug-gang members talk to BBC
Warning: Strong language and descriptions of sexual violence
Although she had just bought hashish from a drug dealer, the woman decided to call the police.
It was because, along with the illegal drugs, she had been handed a note by the young seller during their brief meeting on a Marseille housing estate in 2022.
"We're being held captive and need help. We are 15-years-old," it read.
The teenage dealer, a French court heard earlier this year, was one of two boys being held by a gang which they had both initially approached looking for paid work - albeit illegal.
One boy had been tasked with handling money, the other worked streets around the Frais-Vallon estate. Soon though, bosses had accused them of being responsible for "shortfalls" in takings.
What followed were regular beatings, the court was told, and being forced to dance naked in front of a camera as a form of blackmail. One of the boys was also raped.

Hours after the woman was passed the note, the two teenagers had tried to escape from a second-storey window, injuring themselves in the process. One managed to get away, while the other was caught, beaten and stabbed, but survived.

Arrests were made. Photos on the phone of one of the boys' alleged torturers showed several other young men in a similarly distressed condition. Six men have since been handed hefty sentences for what happened to the two teenagers.
The boys' story highlights the grip that drug gangs hold over parts of France's second city.
While the blend of Mediterranean culture, street art and hip-hop scene has made Marseille a popular tourist destination - beyond the city centre, it is another story.
After months of trying, a BBC team managed to enter this dangerous world - centred on deprived streets and high-rise housing estates in the port city, which police do not enter lightly.
We found an environment where ruthless gangs lure vulnerable young people with promises of easy money, but end up trapping them in a world of drug dealing, brutality and exploitation.

We saw how gangs use social media to recruit hitmen and spoke to several young men caught up in the violence. From prison, one gang member accused of involvement in several murders explained how his "cold-bloodedness" had helped him rise through the ranks.
A still image from one of DZ Mafia's notorious video statements
The city's most powerful gang, DZ Mafia, emerged victorious from a bloody turf war and is now one of the most feared criminal organisations in France.
DZ is the official internet country code for Algeria, where one of the gang's founders, a French-Algerian called Mehdi Laribi, was detained earlier this year under a French arrest warrant.

The criminal outfit rose to prominence in 2023, when it became the first French gang to capitalise on its notoriety by releasing video statements - using social media to market itself as a brand - says the head of the country's anti-drug trafficking unit, Dimitri Zoulas.
Its most recent statement came in July, when the mayor of a nearby town had to be placed in police protection, after intelligence suggested he was in danger of being targeted by the group.
In an online video, six masked men dressed in black stood behind a table - as one of them read a statement denying DZ Mafia's involvement.
France's expanding illegal drugs market - which has seen a surge in cocaine imports alongside high volumes of cannabis and synthetic drugs - has also helped the gang grow rapidly.

The number of cocaine users in France is expected soon to reach two million, says Zoulas, up from 600,000 in 2017. Drug smuggling across France generates €7bn (£5.9bn) a year, involving 200,000 people, he adds.

Many of those distributing the drugs are children and the authorities say the number of minors caught up in trafficking is increasing. During 2025, more than 10,000 children were involved in some way, according to official figures.
DZ Mafia is a prime example. To reach more customers, it needs more gang members - more children.
We have found it is now recruiting young people from across France - not just to sell drugs, but to carry out kidnap, torture and murder.
They are a generation seen as easy to corrupt, but also expendable, by the kingpins who typically control them from prison or overseas.
And, as police and judges warn, once these children enter Marseille's underworld, it is very hard to get them out.
Karine was called by a doctor about her son Hugo: "Your son arrived last night. He took a bullet to the head"
Few know the human cost of Marseille's gangs like mother Karine Brouillard - who lives at the other end of France, almost as far from the Mediterranean coast as you can get.

Her son, Hugo, first ran away aged 15 - from his home in a village in the Nord department - after an argument with his family. He was picked up by police three days later, almost 1,000km (600 miles) away in Marseille, with money and cannabis on him. He was taken home.
But several years later, in 2023, Hugo planned to return south, telling his parents he had secured a holiday job at a restaurant near Marseille.
"He gave regular updates," Karine remembers. "He called me, everything was going well."
Three weeks later, a doctor called. Karine says she will never forget his words: "Your son arrived last night. He took a bullet to the head."
Police believe Hugo was brought for medical help from a gang-controlled area and suspect he was involved with one.
DZ Mafia wields power in Marseille's Quartier Nord
Our best way into Quartier Nord, where DZ Mafia wields power, is with the help of resident Fadella Ouidef, a 41-year-old mother-of-four who gives us a tour.
Thirty-seven seconds after entering one housing estate, we find ourselves cornered.

Car horns sound the moment Fadella's Peugeot passes a gang checkpoint - the teenagers manning the post immediately spot our camera. "Wait, stop filming," Fadella warns, as a grey 4x4 forces us to the side of the road.
"I'm making a report for my housing association," she tells the inquisitive driver. He eventually agrees to let us leave if we stop filming.
It is unnerving to see a non-police vehicle move so assertively and a relief to watch it leave.
"Lately, the gangs have been very aggressive," explains Fadella. "What we simply try to do is make sure our young people understand what's happening is wrong."
Fadella speaks to a wider fear among local families: that their children are enticed by huge sums of money to take a criminal path that robs them of their innocence.
Camil, who claims to have left DZ Mafia, only agreed to speak to the BBC away from the city - on a boat
Money is what led one young man to spend his teenage years with DZ Mafia.
In order for our interviewees to speak freely, or because of safety concerns, we have agreed to protect their identities.
Camil tells us he worked up the gang's ranks to "running security" in one area it controls.
The now 20-year-old, who claims to have left the group, is highly suspicious of our presence, but agrees to tell us how the gang recruits young members.
"They know how to get inside your head. Whatever you want, they give to you," he says. This can range from nice cars and spacious apartments, to drugs and prostitutes, he explains.
"You feel loyalty because of what they give you. You'll stay until the very end, until either death or prison."
Camil also gives a sobering assessment of what happens if the gang identifies a weakness in a recruit: "They'll exploit it. You're their bitch, it's over."
DZ Mafia member, Adam - not his real name - tells us he was part of a DZ Mafia hit squad when we speak to him in a Snapchat video call.
He is currently in prison awaiting trial, after being implicated in several murders.
"People noticed my determination, my cold-bloodedness and, without wanting to, I climbed up the ladder of the gang," says Adam. "It became my place, I had to roll with it."
During the chat, he agrees the killings he has been charged with were "quite shocking".

"Attempts in broad daylight, in traffic jams… it can range from going to hit a guy, slap him to taking him in front of his mother and burning him up in a car. I think I have good composure, I handle it fairly well."
"Thank you, see you soon" reads graffiti on a wall, alongside price lists for cocaine, hashish and marijuana
We challenge Adam on whether he feels regret when carrying out such acts of brutality.
He says he is "feeling in-part guilty" but claims to have no regrets.
"If I hadn't done all of this, there are other people who would have done that in my place, and so on. I am just another brick in the wall," he says.

articles.title: Jensen Huang: Why a personal scandal for the face of the AI boom has provoked a national security scare
articles.summary: Once lauded as the "Taylor Swift of tech", Huang is mired in scandal after an affair with a suspected Chinese spy.
body: Jensen Huang is one of the technology industry's most high-profile figures.
He rose to prominence as the business he leads - artificial intelligence (AI) chip giant Nvidia - became one of the world's most valuable companies.
As the face of the AI boom, Huang also became close to Donald Trump as the president pushed for the US to keep its dominance of the technology over China.
The 63-year-old who was once lauded as the "Taylor Swift of tech" and referred to as "Daddy Huang" in Taiwan is now mired in scandal after an affair with a suspected Chinese spy.
Born in Taiwan in 1963, Huang was nine years old when his family moved to the West Coast of the US.
He graduated as an electrical engineer from Oregon State University, and then with a master's degree in the same field from Stanford University.
Huang then worked at US chip firm AMD before co-founding Nvidia.
He has an estimated fortune of $155bn, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index.

"Jensen Huang is a tech visionary of the likes of Steve Jobs," Stephen Witt, the author of Thinking Machine - a biography on Huang, tells the BBC, adding that he was responsible for creating AI hardware as we know it today.
Huang has a famously close relationship with Trump. At the recent AI summit at the White House, where 42 tech executives were present, the president was flanked by Elon Musk and Huang.
Trump said he had not spoken to the Nvidia boss since news of the investigation emerged.
"I just know he's a fine person, but you never know what's going on," Trump told reporters, adding that he had "done an amazing job for our country".
Huang has long found himself at the centre of US-China tensions. Trump has repeatedly said the two nations are in a race for dominance.
Trump has said "whoever wins AI wins", and the fear is that if China gains the upper hand in AI, it will supercharge the country's military and surveillance capabilities.

The US advantage is in large part because of US companies like Nvidia, working with producers like the Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC), which makes more than 90% of the world's most advanced chips.
Since 2022 the US has used various export controls to keep the top tech out of China, which it says helps retain America's competitive edge and protects its national security.

But it means companies like Nvidia have been largely locked out of the world's most lucrative market, with Jensen Huang once saying that Nvidia's share of the Chinese market had gone from around 95% to effectively zero. In recent years Huang has engaged in a flurry of shuttle diplomacy, dashing between Washington and Beijing, hoping to find a US-approved way back in, and shaping US policy on China along the way.
Sunday's revelations may explain why Huang has failed to bring home the biggest prize of all to Nvidia: the Trump administration's blessing to sell all but its most advanced chips to China.
Quarter after quarter of late, Nvidia has been locked out of that lucrative market. Despite his ostensible closeness to Trump, Huang has not managed to wrest this concession from the administration.
Huang is commonly referred to as "Daddy Huang" in Taiwan where he was born
Huang founded Nvidia with fellow electrical engineers Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem in 1993.
The company was originally known for chips that process graphics, particularly for computer games.
Eventually it changed focus to AI, a field it now dominates.

"In 2012 these machine learning neural net researchers started to use it for that purpose and Jensen immediately recognised that this was going to be a massive industry and the future of computing. He began to pour enormous amounts of resources into building what was essentially the AI hardware market," says Witt.

"Today when we think of that, we think of these giant data centres - none of that existed. There were no customers for the stuff he was building. In fact his first customer was Open AI at the time they had 30 people - he actually gave it to them, he donated it to them."
Nvidia is now worth some $4.5 trillion, making it one of the most valuable companies ever.

"The first real neural net of modern times on an Nvidia network was Alex Krizhevsky's Alexnet and they trained that on two Nvidia cards in Alex's bedroom. Now we do the same thing but we do it with 200,000 - 300,000 cards and instead of doing it in a bedroom we do it in a giant barn full of computers called a data centre," adds Witt.

"So when you think about a data centre buildout, when you hear the AI infrastructure buildout, Jensen runs a tollbooth. All of that goes through him. And it made his company at least temporarily, the most valuable company in the world."
Nvidia's board has announced a probe following reports by the New York Times that Huang had engaged in a romantic relationship with a woman believed by US intelligence to be a Chinese spy.
For now, though, Nvidia's board appears to have little appetite for removing Huang, saying in a statement on Sunday that they have "confidence in Jensen and his leadership team".
Sources tell the BBC his removal is unlikely because there is so much money at stake. There is also no clear successor to the 63-year old tech boss.
Huang met his wife Lori at Oregon State University, where she was also studying electrical engineering and was his lab partner.
They married in 1985, about eight years before he co-founded Nvidia, and have two children, Madison and Spencer.
He has credited Lori and Madison for making black leather jackets his signature style.
Lori Huang accompanied her husband at the state dinner held by President Donald Trump for his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping in September
In 2007, the couple founded the Jen-Hsun and Lori Huang Foundation.
The charitable fund has seen its assets surge in recent years, driven by the soaring value of Nvidia shares, and is estimated to be worth more than $9bn.
Its donations include tens of millions of dollars to engineering programmes at Oregon State and Stanford University.
"Jensen in my conversations with him and in other conversations has gone to great lengths to present himself as a family man. That's very important to him," says Witt.

"He praises his wife, he talks about her in very glowing ways. Both of his children work for Nvidia. Spencer and Maddison. The fallout of this would be bad for anyone's family. But for someone who has gone to such great lengths to cultivate an image of being a family guy and who keeps his children very close, it is very bad."
Huang for his part released a statement which said, "I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry."
US officials had concluded that Alice Huang had been recruited to spy by China's top intelligence agency, the New York Times reports.

She was a top executive at Megaspeed, a data centre company based in Singapore. The firm had been suspected of helping divert Nvidia chips to China, a concern that Nvidia maintains was investigated and debunked.
Surveillance reportedly revealed communications between Alice Huang and an American citizen, who was subsequently identified as Jensen Huang through a process known as "unmasking".
It remains unclear what information Alice Huang – who is also known as Huang Le – allegedly passed to Beijing, how valuable it was, or when she is believed to have begun gathering intelligence.
Alice Huang did not respond to the paper's request for comment.
When the BBC asked Nvidia if the company was aware of intelligence concerns, the company said it was not.
"We trust that if we were the target of a genuine threat, the US government would have notified us," an Nvidia spokesperson told the BBC.
Additional reporting by Ayeshea Perera in Singapore and Helen Davidson in Sydney

articles.title: US officials seek ‘final end’ to Russia-Ukraine war as Abu Dhabi talks begin
articles.summary: First substantive peace talks since February to include US proposal for ‘long-term security architecture’ between Moscow and Europe
body: US officials have said they are seeking a “final end” to the war between Russia and Ukraine, beginning with trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday, the first substantive negotiations between the two countries since February.
The talks are the first since the US launched joint strikes with Israel against Iran, and they follow bruising midterm elections that have weakened Donald Trump at home.
Part of the Trump administration’s proposal involves drawing up a new “long-term security architecture” between Russia and Europe, administration officials have said.

European officials are concerned that Russia may stick to its hardline demands that Nato should roll back its military footprint across eastern Europe, which would threaten to leave allies vulnerable to Moscow’s influence at a time of historic tensions with the west.

Before the trilateral talks, European officials held separate discussions on Tuesday with representatives from Ukraine and the US, where they agreed “any future arrangements must respect sovereignty, territorial integrity, independent decision-making, and provide credible security guarantees for Ukraine”, according to a joint statement.

European leaders are not convinced Russia intends to negotiate in good faith. “So far they have just been pretending that they negotiate because we haven’t seen any ⁠goodwill from the Russian side,” the EU high representative for foreign policy, Kaja Kallas, told Reuters on Monday.

European countries want to be involved in discussions, although there are signs of unease about the proliferating strands of peace talks. Italy’s prime minister, Giorgia Meloni, last week complained about the “disorderly” process of meetings and phone calls that she argued weakened Europe’s ability to speak with one voice.

Since his first decade in power, Vladimir Putin has complained about Nato’s eastward expansion and sought to renegotiate the balance of power between Nato and Russia – but never before have those demands been embraced by a sitting US administration, which has made it clear that it is desperate to get to a deal.

Previewing the discussions, a US administration official said the US would “need Europe at the table” to end the war. He said negotiators could also revive the Nato-Russian council that was suspended after Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022, and potentially lift sanctions against Russia to get to a deal.

The US officials also claimed that they had discussed with Russia potential security guarantees to Ukraine similar to Nato’s article 5, which protects member states in case of an attack. Russia has strongly opposed Nato admitting Ukraine or western countries placing troops in Ukraine.
“What they would be getting would be effectively very similar to Nato,” an administration official said.

“Getting a US security guarantee is a really, really big deal,” the official added, saying it would be up to Donald Trump and Ukraine’s Volodymyr Zelenskyy to discuss. “And if he wants to do that, that’s that’s a very, very big deal in terms of resources and funding and military support.”

Critics have expressed skepticism about what may trigger those security guarantees, however, noting that article 5 does not oblige Nato member states to defend others, and that cyber-attacks and other forms of hybrid warfare have blurred the line for what would require a military response.

Jared Kushner, Trump’s son-in-law and a lead negotiator for the US, described a potential new framework for Europe in general terms on Monday, saying the US would seek “stronger consultation, reliable crisis communications, greater military transparency, and reciprocal measures to reduce escalation risks, while fully respecting the sovereignty and independent decision-making of every nation”.

European delegations from Germany, France, the UK, Italy and the EU will meet US negotiators in Abu Dhabi to discuss the “long-term security architecture between Russia and Europe in order to figure out how to reduce future conflicts”.

A European security official from a country attending the talks said that the US proposal was not yet clear and that they were bracing themselves for the US to pose serious concessions to Russia during the Abu Dhabi consultations.

“We already have a European security architecture in place,” said Kallas at a G7 foreign ministers meeting on Monday. “This includes international agreements under which Russia has undertaken obligations, including with regard to sovereignty and territorial integrity. The problem is that Russia is not respecting these agreements.”
Donald Trump has also said that Ukraine would like be expected to give up territory in a final deal, and would end with a “little bit different shape”.

After meeting the Kremlin adviser Kirill Dmitriev last week, Trump said he would seek a “big, beautiful agreement” that “might involve all of Europe”. Critics are concerned that Trump and Putin could try to go over the heads of European leaders in order to negotiate a peace that gives serious concessions to Russia.

“There’s a lot of baggage that people in Europe have about this idea,” said a US administration official, pointing specifically to Russia’s 2021 proposal that was viewed as an ultimatum to Nato to get out of eastern Europe.

At that time, Russia issued a list of demands to Nato that included a ban on expansion to new countries including Ukraine, a rollback of troops to its pre-1997 borders, and limits on where it could place missiles. Nato rejected that proposal, and Russia invaded Ukraine less than a month later.

The US administration official said: “We have to build something new that works today … Because if all the old architecture was working well, then we wouldn’t be in this long war. And so obviously something’s not working, and we need to come up with a way that when we end this war, it really is a final end to the war.”
The content of those proposals are not clear yet, although the secretary of state, Marco Rubio, claimed on Monday “there’s been some advances made in what that architecture should look”.
“We obviously have to get past the conflict to get to that point,” he added.

articles.title: Disgraced former leader Sheikh Hasina plans return to Bangladesh from exile
articles.summary: Former prime minister faces death penalty upon return after being sentenced in absentia over deaths in 2024 uprising
body: Sheikh Hasina is “confident” she will return to Bangladesh in December, according to exiled members of her party, after the disgraced former prime minister of Bangladesh applied for a new passport this week.

Hasina has been living in self-imposed exile since August 2024 when she was toppled from power by a mass uprising against her authoritarian rule. She crossed the border to India, where she has since been allowed to live freely in Delhi.
Related: Bangladesh student protests turn into ‘mass movement against a dictator’
Last November, a tribunal in Bangladesh found Hasina guilty of crimes against humanity and sentenced her to death over her crackdown on a student uprising that left an estimated 1,400 people dead.

Her return to Bangladesh is likely to be disruptive for the country where Hasina’s party, Awami League, is still banned and thousands of its members are in jail. Should she be allowed to return, she is likely to be arrested immediately.
Related: The exiled Awami league members plotting a political comeback in Bangladesh – from India

Hasina first raised the prospect of going back to Bangladesh in August. Speaking to the Guardian this week, several exiled Awami League leaders also living in India confirmed that Hasina was serious and “confident” about returning by next month. They confirmed that several other party figures had already returned in anticipation.

On Monday, a British lawyer acting on behalf of Hasina wrote to the Bangladesh high commission in Delhi requesting a new passport and national identity card to be issued “in a timely fashion”, in a letter seen by the Guardian.

“The reason our leader Sheikh Hasina has applied for a passport is that she genuinely wants to return,” said a party leader based in the Indian city of Kolkata, who spoke on condition of anonymity because he is not authorised to speak to the media on the party’s behalf.

Hasina has rejected the charges against her and claimed the tribunal that convicted her was illegitimate. “She is confident about her return, which is why she has applied for a new passport and a national identity card. If the authorities do not issue her a passport, she will apply for a travel pass to make her return to Bangladesh possible,” said the Awami League leader.

Since Hasina’s conviction, the Bangladesh government has put pressure on the Indian authorities to extradite the former prime minister. However, the Indian government, which was close to Hasina while she was in power, has ignored the demands, straining ties between the two countries.
This week, the Bangladesh government said that, as a “terrorist”, Hasina would only be allowed to return via an “acceptable prisoner exchange” under the India-Bangladesh extradition treaty.
Aminul Islam, the chief prosecutor of the tribunal that sentenced Hasina, said there was “no legal scope” for her to be issued a new passport as she was a “convicted fugitive”.

Islam emphasised that Hasina would be hanged if she returned, as the deadline for her to appeal against her conviction had passed. “Sheikh Hasina has no option but to face the execution of the verdict,” he said.
Despite her conviction and the party’s ban, Hasina still commands significant popularity among the thousands of Awami League cadre still in Bangladesh, many of whom have been driven underground.

Analysts said they believed her decision to return was driven by an attempt to revive her support base and destabilise the newly elected government, led by Tarique Rahman. It came to power in February during Bangladesh’s first democratic election in decades.
The government has since struggled with inflation and protests that shut down garment factories, which the Awami League hopes to use to its advantage.

Another Awami League leader said all those in exile intended to follow Hasina back to Bangladesh, despite many of them facing serious criminal charges and having been given lengthy prison sentences in absentia.

“Some of us have been sentenced in absentia by kangaroo courts, and we know we will be jailed. But we are ready to face the consequences and return to our own people. We will fight this politically,” said the senior leader, who is based in India.

Some senior party figures have returned in recent months, including the former MP Mustaque Ahmed Ruhi. He was immediately arrested on his return in September and faces prosecution over an alleged murder during the 2024 uprising.
Exiled Awami League leaders have continued to meet in Kolkata, where many of them are living, and are routinely summoned to Delhi to meet Hasina.
Speaking over email this week, Hasina told the Associated Press: “If death is my destiny, I would rather die on the soil of my own country, among my own people.”

articles.title: ‘We are human too’: the Roma film-makers striking back at stereotypes
articles.summary: Seven films in Seville programme highlight how Roma are creating their own narratives
body: Growing up in Romania, whenever Alina Șerban spotted Roma people on television or in movies, they were usually cast as villains or depicted as somehow exotic.

But this week the Romany actor and film-maker is part of a cohort pushing back against this stereotyping, joining forces with Romany film-makers from across Europe in a landmark screening of seven films during the Seville European film festival.
“It’s work made by us, not just about us,” said Șerban. “I was raised in a world where everything I heard about my community came from the exterior … The perspective is finally being centred.”

Her film, I Matter, which tells the story of a young woman who reckons with her Romany identity as she comes of age, was screened earlier this year as part of the Venice film festival’s spotlight section, where it won the audience award.

It was a triumph for a film that Șerban had envisioned as a way to build bridges towards “a different understanding” of Romany people, who rank among Europe’s most marginalised communities, with longstanding discrimination leading to challenges in accessing decent housing and the segregation of children in schools.
“I wanted to show, in a very simple but complex manner, that we are human too,” she said. “I’m claiming Roma humanity.”

Organisers described this week’s showcase, titled Raising Romani Gaze and housed within the wider Seville festival, as the first of its kind. “This is something that we have been building up to for around 10 years,” said Katalin Bársony, a Romany film-maker from Hungary and one of the curators of the programme.

The wide range of talent in the community as well as a willingness in the industry to recognise their narratives had made it possible now. “Romany people, despite being the biggest minority in Europe, we are one of the most underserved and invisible when it comes to our own art that we create,” said Bársony, who also leads the Romédia Foundation, an NGO which seeks to use storytelling, film and visual archives to strengthen Roma self-representation and challenge prejudices.

The result was a programme that offered an unprecedented glimpse of Europe’s richness by giving “narrative sovereignty” to some of the estimated 10-12 million Roma who live across Europe, she said. “From the start of the silent film, Romany people have been put in certain roles. And those roles were mostly passive and defined by the outside gaze.”

The films range from a documentary by Bársony that follows a young man born in Germany to Roma parents and who is deported to Kosovo, to a film by the Spanish director Jero de los Santos that delves into queer and Romany perspectives.

The showcase also includes Smooth the Edges, by the Nottingham-based Romany film-maker Charles Newland. “It’s a bit of an outlier,” said Newland, “because it’s the first film funded by the British Film Institute by a Romany director with a Romany producer and a lead Romany cast.”

The short captures a dilemma that Newland described as common in Britain’s Romany community: that of a young woman who wrestles with whether to hide her background in order to avoid workplace discrimination. What emerges is the tension in the trade-off of being able to escape discrimination but at a cost of repressing part of herself. The film also sought to engage with the in-between world that Roma in the UK were often forced to reckon with, said Newland.

“Especially politically, there are a lot of people who can be racist against my group of people, but then on the same token, when it suits their argument, refer to you as white as well,” he said. “Sort of like, ‘oh they’re just Gypsies, they’re scum’ when it suits that agenda, but if it’s an agenda of trying to help out, it’s like, ‘well, why do they need help because they’re just white people?’ So you get stuck between this rock and a hard place.”

By bringing together Roma film-makers from across Europe, this week’s programme also offers a chance to push back against what has unfortunately become a common thread in the lives of many Roma across the continent, said Șerban. “As they say, the last form of acceptable racism is towards Roma people,” she said. “Being Roma for me, at least in the Romanian context, and for my generation, meant that you were somehow inferior.”

Against that backdrop, every decision she took on her film felt like an “act of resistance”, she said. “Hopefully, in some years’ time, there will be 50 or 100 films like mine. But since I was one of the first to bring this perspective, I had all this pressure and all these nuances to think about. You become an ambassador without choosing to be one.”

She saw it as a necessary step, however, in seizing the chance to tell stories that could allow audiences to see Roma living complex human experiences while also allowing Roma to see themselves on screen as more than just stereotypes. “Films bring change,” she said. “Art makes people think of how life is for another person.”
The Raising Romani Gaze programme will run at the 23rd Seville European film festival from 10 to 14 November 2026

articles.title: Tuesday briefing: The world is falling short on climate action. Can Cop31 change that?
articles.summary: In today’s newsletter: As global leaders gather in Turkey for the UN climate summit, both doubts and hope surround what the annual talks can achieve
body: Good morning. After another year of unprecedented droughts, floods and wildfires driven by human-caused global heating, 91 heads of government will meet tomorrow in Turkey to discuss the climate crisis. They will do so against a backdrop of global instability and conflict.

But as high-ranking officials and civil society campaigners settle in for a fortnight of speeches, protests and labyrinthine negotiations at the UN’s 31st annual climate conference, Cop31, many are asking what the point is.

Those same governments pledged more than a decade ago in Paris, at Cop21, to limit global heating to 1.5C above preindustrial levels, but implementation has been sclerotic, and only two months ago a UN report warned temperatures will reach at least 1.8C using even the most optimistic future projections.

I spoke to the Guardian’s environment editor Fiona Harvey in Turkey about what’s on the Cop31 agenda, what success looks like and why Brazil’s re-elected president Lula will be the star of the conference.
UK | Russell Brand was sentenced to more than 10 years in prison on Monday after a judge praised his victims’ bravery and accused him of living “unhindered by the rules by which decent people live”.

US | Donald Trump, Elon Musk and prominent finance moguls have expressed their support for embattled Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, as the head of the world’s most valuable chip company faces an internal investigation over a romantic relationship with an alleged Chinese spy.

Russia | US officials said they would seek a “final end” to the war between Russia and Ukraine, beginning with trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday in the first substantive negotiations between the two countries since February.
Technology | Palantir lobbied a health minister to consider extending its AI technology into GP records, stretching its reach into the NHS in a way doctors fear could undermine trust with patients.
Climate | Soaring oil and gas prices following the war in Iran have encouraged people to look beyond fossil fuels, leading to an easing of climate-damaging carbon emissions this year.
The 31st Conference of the Parties to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change – or Cop31 – is taking place in the Turkish coastal city of Antalya until 20 November.

The conference centre – which, as at every Cop meeting, is temporarily designated UN international territory and policed by UN security officers – is set on the outskirts of the city. At this time of year, it is usually the venue for a global conference of plastic surgeons, part of a billion-dollar industry in Turkey.

But this week and next it will host an estimated 70,000 registered delegates, from the professional lanyard class to civil society campaigners. When we spoke at lunchtime, Fiona had already spotted Indigenous groups from the Amazon, Australia and the Pacific in national dress – a colourful sight at every Cop, where indigenous delegates know they can attract significant media attention.

When I reported with Fiona from Cop26 in Glasgow, five years ago, inclusivity was a major theme, with observers from Indigenous communities, trade unions and environmental NGOs complained that they had not been given sufficient access to formal negotiating spaces, and staged a symbolic walkout on the final day.

This is a long-running argument, says Fiona, alongside running questions about the scope for campaigners to host protests and alternative gatherings around the conference venue. “Four out of five of the last Cops were held in countries with repressive regimes,” she reminds me, where scope for outside dissent was very limited.

Annual Cop summits rotate between countries from different regions of the world, but this year a rancorous dispute between Turkey and Australia has resulted in an unhappy compromise. Turkey is the official host and in charge of the action agenda, the “jolly bits” that surround the voluntary agreements, rather than the tension of formal negotiations.

Australia is in charge of those, which will see countries thrash out the details of just transition and climate finance programmes. This is “the short straw” says Fiona, with none of the pleasing global focus of physical hosting, and with climate advocates questioning Australia’s credibility to manage these negotiations as a major fossil fuel producer. Although Turkey is hardly a better fit: as Fiona puts it, “The one thing they have in common is their mutual admiration for coal.”

Formal negotiations this year will mainly be focused on the just transition mechanism, which aims to ensure people who are working in fossil fuel industries aren’t completely abandoned in the move to renewable energy, as well as helping poorer countries - who happen to be significantly less responsible for the climate crisis – to access enough finance to deal with the worsening climate crisis.

This year, Fiona has sensed less urgency from global leaders over Cop31. Alongside the anticipated absence of the Trump White House, as well as China’s Xi Jinping and India’s Narendra Modi, there are some other disappointing no-shows. The UK’s Andy Burnham is due to arrive, alongside the EU’s Ursula von der Leyen, but the French president, Emmanuel Macron, and the German chancellor Friedrich Mertz will not attend, nor will Canada’s Mark Carney.

Fiona also questions whether the Cop process is fit for purpose. “The negotiation processes are endlessly convoluted and cause their own problems. It took more than five years just to negotiate the Paris ‘rulebook’ under which the treaty is put into effect. And the convention that all resolutions must pass by consensus has given petrostates free rein to obstruct progress,” she says.

But Fiona, a Cop optimist, says there are two places where progress can be made. The first is through the informal discussions, known as the action agenda, which generate voluntary commitments alongside the binding commitments under Paris. The second, the part of the formal negotiations known as the “cover decision”. Some of the “really dynamite” advances from previous Cops can be found in this text – such as the agreement to transition away from fossil fuels, which every single country signed up to at last year’s Cop30 in Brazil. This year, Brazil’s president, Lula, is expected to bring a plan for how to make that happen.***
What could be achieved at this year’s conference?

The UN argues that rapid action to cut greenhouse gas emissions would limit the Paris agreement overshoot and bring down global temperatures by the end of this century. This can’t happen without a transition away from fossil fuels and the Brazilian delegation is bringing a detailed global roadmap for how this can be done – though it won’t be part of the formal negotiations..

While the Brazil roadmap does not include a timetable for phasing out fossil fuels, it is still an important contribution as it sets out the different dilemmas that countries face – such as losing tax revenues by cutting fossil fuel use, for instance, or axing subsidies which might have helped poorer households. “This means governments can recognise the issues they will face in their transition, as well as the benefits, and plan accordingly,” says Fiona.

The talks will also seek support for a new 2035 electrification goal, backed by Turkey and Australia, under which 35% of final energy use around the world coming from electricity instead of fossil fuels.

This comes as China’s oil imports, for instance, are likely to be down about 12% this year, in part owing to a massive uptake of electric vehicles, with many other countries following suit – but not the UK it seems. As we reported exclusively yesterday, ministers are expected to make steep cuts to the government’s EV targets – their biggest decarbonisation policy – in a move that will alarm many Labour MPs who are concerned about the government’s commitment to the green agenda and may be embarrassing for Burnham as he flies into a conference with electrification so high on the agenda. Some experts argue that the inbuilt efficiency of electric tech compared with fossil fuels means that a global switch to electrification would halve energy demand around the world.

China – still one of the world’s biggest polluters – is dominating energy transition with some astonishing results: its renewable generation capacity has now outstripped coal, saving billions of dollars for consumers and businesses as the oil price soars. And solar is booming in Africa at last, adds Fiona.

The re-election of President Lula has buoyed climate activists everywhere, who take hope from his success in beating far-right populism with an unashamedly climate-focused agenda, which aims to secure the vitally important Amazon rainforest for future generations.
This is his first international trip since last month’s electoral triumph, and Fiona predicts he’ll receive “a stupendous welcome.”

His presence is also important as a vocal champion of climate justice. “He says very clearly it’s the elites, of both developed and developing nations, who are responsible for the biggest emissions with their high carbon lifestyles and investments in fossil fuel companies, not the ordinary people”.

We’ll likely hear more from him about his proposals for a potentially transformative global wealth tax – at previous international summits Brazil has argued for a 2% tax on those with assets worth more than $1bn. “He wants the people who have benefited from this to pay. It’s a hugely powerful message. How can you argue against that?”
